screens.title: UART Communication Between Devices
screens.subtitle: Configure UART1 on two LaunchPads, send packets, detect errors, and verify integrity with a checksum.

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on using UART to connect two embedded boards directly, not just for PC debugging. You will learn how to configure UART1 on the TM4C123G, wire two LaunchPads in a null modem arrangement, and design a compact packet protocol with a start byte, command byte, data byte, and checksum. We’ll also cover common UART errors — frame, overrun, and parity — and how to detect them with the UART error register and respond by discarding corrupted packets and requesting retransmission. A concrete example shows a master board sending a toggle-LED command to a slave board with checksum verification. Why this matters: device-to-device UART is a simple, reliable way to move small control messages between modules such as sensors and controllers. By the end of the lesson you’ll be able to wire TX to RX, configure baud and FIFOs for UART1, implement send and receive routines, calculate and verify a checksum, and handle errors so your system recovers from noise or timing problems. Ready to explore wiring, code, protocol, and troubleshooting step by step?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will gain and how each maps to a verified milestone.

narration.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to configure two LaunchPads to communicate over UART1, send and receive packeted data, implement a simple checksum-based protocol to detect corruption, and handle common UART errors. First, configuring UART1 means selecting PB0 and PB1 pins, setting baud and enabling transmit and receive so a master board can drive messages and a slave board can read them. Second, sending and receiving packets requires tight send and wait logic so the receiver reads bytes in the correct order. Third, implementing a packet format with start, command, data, and checksum gives you a rule that both sides follow to verify integrity. Finally, handling frame, overrun, and parity errors means checking the UART error register after reads and taking corrective action such as discarding and requesting retransmission. Each objective includes a small milestone you can verify during the hands-on lab, like a successful LED toggle command acknowledged with a checksum-verified response. These skills let small modules coordinate reliably without a PC in the loop.

screens.title: What device-to-device UART means
screens.subtitle: Definition, use cases, and a common wiring misconception explained.

narration.text: Device-to-device UART means two microcontroller boards exchange serial data directly over a pair of transmit and receive lines plus a shared ground. Unlike PC debugging where UART0 is connected to a USB interface, device links use a separate module such as UART1 so the debug console remains available. A common use case is a sensor module sending periodic readings to a main controller, or two controllers sharing commands to coordinate motors. The critical wiring rule is TX of one board must connect to RX of the other and vice versa; this crossover, often called a null modem, lets each transmitter feed the other’s receiver. A widely seen misconception is to wire TX to TX because labels look similar; that will result in no meaningful data transfer. Another subtle point is ground: without a shared reference, signal levels are meaningless and communications fail even if TX/RX are crossed correctly. A quick mental check is to trace the signal path: transmitter output pin → receiver input pin → common ground reference. Can you picture why swapping TX/RX stops all traffic? What device-to-device UART means means null modem wiring plus a common ground is the simplest physical requirement for board-to-board uart.. Definition
Two microcontrollers exchange asynchronous serial bytes directly using UART modules and shared ground.
Use case
Sensor module reports readings to a main controller, which uses the data to adjust outputs in real time.
Key rule
TX of A → RX of B, RX of A ← TX of B, and connect GNDs. This null modem crossover is mandatory.
Common mistake
Wiring TX to TX instead of crossing TX/RX. It appears connected but no data is received.
Concrete example
Two LaunchPads: use UART1 on PB0 (RX) and PB1 (TX) on each board. Connect PB1 of board A to PB0 of board B, PB1 of B to PB0 of A, and connect both grounds. With that wiring, a character sent by board A appears at board B's receive buffer.
Key Takeaway

Cross TX and RX and share ground. If nothing is received, check wiring and ground first before changing code.

screens.title: Wiring two LaunchPads for UART1
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step wiring checklist to establish the physical link.

narration.text: A reliable physical link starts with a disciplined checklist. Step one is identify UART1 pins: on the TM4C123G, UART1 typically uses PB0 for receive and PB1 for transmit. Step two is crossing transmit and receive: connect PB1 of Board A to PB0 of Board B and PB1 of Board B to PB0 of Board A. Step three is tying grounds: connect both board grounds so the voltage levels have a common reference. Step four is leave UART0 alone for the debug console; keep PC logging available while you test the inter-board link. When performing the wiring, use short, direct jumper wires and avoid wiring TX to TX; a common mistake is to assume similarly labeled pins should be paired. A practical check after wiring is to use a simple send routine from one board and a receive routine on the other to verify a single known byte. If the byte does not appear, re-check ground and crossing before adjusting baud rate. This stepwise discipline prevents time-consuming chase after the wrong layer of the system. screens.title: Send and receive routines for UART1
screens.subtitle: Blocking send and receive functions that wait on FIFO status.

narration.text: Reliable byte transfer often uses simple blocking functions that wait until the transmitter or receiver is ready. The send function waits until the transmit FIFO is not full, then writes the character to the data register. The receive function waits until a byte is available, then reads the data register. This simple pattern avoids dropped bytes when the receiver polls fast enough. In practice you use status flags: a transmit full flag prevents writes until space exists, and a receive empty flag prevents reads until data arrives. The code shown in the lesson uses hardware flags named for the TM4C series; the send routine waits until the TX full flag clears, then assigns the character to the UART data register. The receive routine waits until the RX is not empty, then reads the data register and returns the lowest eight bits as a char. A common misconception is that non-blocking code always scales better. For tiny control messages, blocking routines are simpler and sufficient — only move to interrupts or DMA when you need high throughput or low latency multitasking. Try these blocking routines during the initial lab to confirm correct wiring and baud before adding complexity.

keyIdea.title: Blocking I/O
keyIdea.text: Blocking send/receive is simple and reliable for short command packets during initial testing.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Send and receive routines for UART1
Reference Routines
Blocking routines that poll hardware flags before performing I/O.
void UART1_SendChar(char c) {
    while ((UART1_FR_R & UART_FR_TXFF) != 0) {}
    UART1_DR_R = c;
}

char UART1_ReceiveChar(void) {
    while ((UART1_FR_R & UART_FR_RXFE) != 0) {}  // Wait for data
    return (char)(UART1_DR_R & 0xFF);
}
These functions wait on the transmit full and receive empty flags so data writes and reads occur safely. Use them as a baseline before moving to interrupts.
Explanation bullets
  • While loop checks hardware flag to avoid read/write hazards.
  • Writing UART data register transmits the byte onto TX line.
  • Reading UART data register returns the received byte; mask to 0xFF for the data byte.
  • Block until ready works well for short command packets and initial testing.
Pro tip
If you plan concurrent tasks, migrate to interrupt-driven receive to avoid busy-wait CPU usage.

screens.title: Baud rate and frame errors
screens.subtitle: Why baud mismatch causes frame errors and how to check for them.

narration.text: Baud rate is the speed at which bits are sent over the UART line. Both boards must use the same baud, otherwise the receiver samples bits at incorrect times and may miss the stop bit. When the stop bit is not detected or is sampled incorrectly, hardware reports a frame error. This is a basic symptom of mismatched baud settings. A concrete example: if one board is set to 115200 and the other to 9600, their bit timing differs dramatically and the receiver will rarely reconstruct valid bytes. A common misconception is that minor baud differences are harmless; small mismatches can still produce intermittent frame errors and corrupt packets. To diagnose, verify both boards' baud configuration before altering wiring or code. Logging frame errors and checking the UART error register after reads will reveal whether timing, not wiring, is the likely problem. Fixing the baud alignment typically resolves many mysterious receive failures faster than changing packet parsing code. Baud rate essentials
Bit timing must match on both ends or frames break.

Both sides must be configured to the same baud. A mismatch causes the receiver to sample the bit stream at incorrect times and may miss the stop bit, producing a frame error.

Minor timing differences can lead to sporadic errors; treat baud alignment as the first configuration check.

Diagnostic steps
  • Confirm both UART modules use the same baud setting.
  • Check for frame error flags in the UART error register after a read.
  • When errors appear, reduce baud to a slower rate to simplify testing.
Common mistake
Assuming wiring is wrong when frame errors are really caused by an unmatched baud setting.

screens.title: Designing a simple packet protocol
screens.subtitle: Start byte, command, data, and checksum — structure and example.

narration.text: A protocol gives both sides rules to format and validate messages so commands are unambiguous. A minimal packet used in this chapter has four fields: a start byte that marks the packet boundary, a command byte identifying the action, a data byte carrying the parameter, and a checksum byte computed as the sum of the prior bytes. For example, to tell a slave to turn an LED on you might send 0xAA as the start, 0x01 as the LED control command, 0x01 as data for ON, and a checksum equal to 0xAA plus 0x01 plus 0x01, which produces 0xAC. The receiver checks that the first byte equals the expected start value and then recomputes the checksum; if the sums match, the command executes. This protocol is intentionally simple and efficient for short commands. A common misconception is that checksum equals cryptographic hash; here checksum is only a simple sum to detect common transmission errors. For more robustness you could extend the checksum or add sequence numbers, but the basic four-field packet is sufficient for small control links and easier to implement and debug in the lab.

keyIdea.title: Protocol core
keyIdea.text: Start byte plus a simple additive checksum provides a lightweight integrity check suitable for short command packets.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Designing a simple packet protocol
Packet Structure
A compact packet: start, command, data, checksum.
Start
0xAA
Command
0x01 (LED control)
Data
0x01 (ON)
Checksum
0xAC (sum of prior bytes)
Receiver algorithm: confirm start byte matches the expected marker, read command and data bytes, compute the sum of start, command, and data, and compare to the received checksum. If they match, execute the command; otherwise discard the packet and request retransmission.

screens.title: Checksum verification vs packet discard
screens.subtitle: How receivers decide to accept or reject a packet and why it matters.

narration.text: When a receiver gets bytes it faces a decision: accept the packet and act, or reject it and request retransmission. Checksum verification gives a straightforward rule. After reading the packet you recompute the sum of the start, command, and data bytes and compare it to the received checksum. If they match, the packet is likely intact and you execute the command. If they do not match, the receiver discards the packet. Discarding is important because acting on corrupted commands can cause unsafe or unpredictable behavior. A concrete example: if a corrupted packet flips the data byte that controls motor speed, the result could be a sudden unexpected motion. A common misconception is that a single checksum failure is rare and harmless; in noisy environments repeated checksum mismatches indicate deeper problems like wiring, baud mismatch, or an overrun condition. When discarding, log the failure and request retransmission so the sender can attempt sending the same command again. This conservative approach keeps system behavior predictable and easier to debug. Checksum verification vs packet discard means discard packets with checksum failure and request retransmission to avoid acting on corrupted commands.. In practical terms, how receivers decide to accept or reject a packet and why it matters.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reject on mismatch
keyIdea.text: Discard packets with checksum failure and request retransmission to avoid acting on corrupted commands.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Checksum verification vs packet discard
Accept
When recomputed checksum equals received checksum.
  • Execute command (e.g., toggle LED).
  • Optionally send an acknowledgment to the sender.
  • Log success for monitoring.
Discard
When checksum does not match or packet framing fails.
  • Do not execute the command to avoid unsafe actions.
  • Log the error and request retransmission from the sender.
  • Investigate repeated failures for wiring or baud issues.
Key Takeaway

A simple checksum detects many transmission errors. Prefer rejecting questionable packets and requesting retransmission rather than risking action on bad data.

screens.title: Error detection using the UART error register
screens.subtitle: Frame, overrun, and parity errors and how to read them.

narration.text: UART hardware reports low-level errors that the software should check after reading the data register. The TM4C family provides an error register often referenced as the UART error clear or error status register. Three common flags to monitor are frame error, overrun error, and parity error. A frame error means the expected stop bit was not detected, usually caused by baud mismatch. An overrun error means a new byte arrived before the previous one was read from the receive buffer, often caused by a slow or blocked reader. A parity error indicates the parity bit did not match when parity mode is enabled. The recommended flow is: read the data register, check the error register for any flags, and if any error is set log it and treat the packet as corrupted. For simple implementations you can clear the error flags and request retransmission. A common mistake is to assume reads implicitly clear errors; explicitly check and handle the error register so problems are visible in logs and can be addressed systematically. Error detection using the UART error register means always check the uart error register after reads and treat flagged packets as corrupted.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Error detection using the UART error register
Common UART errors
Frame, overrun, and parity errors affect packet integrity.
Frame error
Stop bit not detected; often baud mismatch.
Overrun
New byte arrived before previous was read; reader too slow.
Parity
Parity bit mismatch when parity mode is enabled.
Handling flow
  1. Read UART data register.
  2. Check UARTECR or error status register for flags.
  3. If any flag set, log and discard packet, then request retransmission.
Explicit error checks make root cause analysis possible and keep your system from acting on corrupted data.

screens.title: Handling corrupted packets and retransmission
screens.subtitle: A conservative flow: detect, discard, notify, and request retransmit.

narration.text: When a packet fails validation the safe course is to avoid executing the command and to ask the sender to try again. A simple handling flow starts with the receiver reading the packet and checking the start byte and checksum. If validation succeeds, respond with an acknowledgment or perform the action. If validation fails or the error register flags an issue, log the failure and notify the sender of the need for retransmission. A minimal notification can be an explicit retransmission request message or a simple absence of acknowledgment, depending on your system design. For example, if a checksum mismatch occurs, the receiver can send a negative acknowledgment so the sender retries the same packet. A common misconception is that the sender should keep blindly resending until success; uncontrolled retries can flood the link. Instead, implement a limited retry count and backoff or require an explicit resend request from the receiver. This structured approach preserves determinism and avoids runaway traffic on a noisy line. Handling corrupted packets and retransmission means discard corrupted packets, notify the sender, and use controlled retries to avoid flooding the link.. In practical terms, a conservative flow: detect, discard, notify, and request retransmit.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Retransmit safely
keyIdea.text: Discard corrupted packets, notify the sender, and use controlled retries to avoid flooding the link.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Handling corrupted packets and retransmission
Retransmission flow
Detect, discard, notify, and retry with limits.
1. Read packet and check start byte and checksum.
2. If valid, execute and optionally send acknowledgment.
3. If invalid or error flags set, log the reason and send a retransmit request.
4. Sender retries with a controlled retry count and optional backoff.
Example scenario
Receiver sees checksum mismatch, sends retransmit request. Sender retries up to a fixed number, then reports failure over debug UART if no acknowledgment arrives.
Pro tip
Log the failure with the error type so you can distinguish wiring issues from transient noise during debugging.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough — toggle LED over UART1

screens.title: Common causes when nothing is received
screens.subtitle: Three likely issues and how to isolate each one.

narration.text: When you wire two LaunchPads and nothing arrives at the receiver, start with three likely causes. First, baud rate mismatch: confirm both UART1 configurations use the exact same baud and framing. Frame errors are a strong indicator of this problem. Second, wiring mistake: TX and RX must be crossed. Verify PB1 on one board is connected to PB0 on the other, not to another TX pin. Also confirm both grounds are tied together. Third, UART module not enabled or wrong pins used: ensure your initialization code targets UART1 and configures PB0 and PB1, not UART0 pins. To isolate the fault, run these checks in order: confirm wiring and ground visually and with a continuity tester, verify UART initialization in code and that UART0 is still available for debug messages, and finally check for frame or overrun errors in the UART error register. A misconception is to spend time rewriting packet parsing before verifying wiring and baud; fix the physical and configuration layers first to save time. Common causes when nothing is received means check wiring and ground, confirm baud and uart initialization, then inspect error flags to identify the root cause.. In practical terms, three likely issues and how to isolate each one.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Check wiring and ground, confirm baud and UART initialization, then inspect error flags to identify the root cause.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Common causes when nothing is received
Three likely causes
Baud mismatch
Frame errors or garbled bytes indicate timing mismatch; confirm both sides share the same baud and framing.
Wiring / Ground
TX/RX wires must be crossed and grounds connected. Check continuity and pin labeling carefully.
Configuration
Ensure your code initializes UART1 and configures PB0/PB1; mistakenly targeting UART0 or wrong pins yields no data.
Isolation order: wiring and ground first, then baud and UART initialization, and finally read error flags to determine whether the issue is timing, buffer overrun, or parity. This ordered approach narrows the search space quickly and prevents wasted debugging effort.

screens.title: What to Remember — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential concepts to carry forward.

narration.text: Keep three core ideas in mind as you build UART links between LaunchPads. First, UART1 configuration is essential: choose PB0 and PB1, set the correct baud, and enable transmit and receive. Second, crossover wiring matters: TX of one board must connect to RX of the other, and both boards must share ground. Third, a simple packet protocol using a start byte, a command, a data byte, and an additive checksum gives a fast, verifiable way to send control messages. These three concepts — correct hardware configuration, correct wiring, and a clear packet format with checksum — form the backbone of reliable device-to-device UART. Use them in that order when you test: first hardware configuration, then wiring, then protocol verification. This practice keeps debugging straightforward and predictable.
